name: Tumescent liposuction

image.caption: Fat removal using cannula during tumescent liposuction

lead: Tumescent liposuction fills fat with a dilute numbing solution before suction, so the patient can stay awake under local anesthesia. It is used on areas such as the abdomen, flanks, neck and jowls for a slimmer, more defined contour, and also for lipedema.

Lidocaine numbs the tissue and epinephrine narrows blood vessels, reducing bleeding and bruising while fat is aspirated through thin cannulas. It was developed by dermatologist Jeffrey Klein in the 1980s and is now a standard technique. Large surveys of dermatologic surgeons have examined its safety, and studies report good long-term results in lipedema.

paras: A surgeon performs it in a procedure room, usually with local anesthesia only. Compression garments are worn afterwards, and the contour shows once swelling settles over weeks.

The literature reports lidocaine toxicity as the technique-specific concern, plus general liposuction risks such as infection, bleeding, clots and contour irregularity. A 1999 report noted deaths and that reporting is not mandatory, so incidence is uncertain.

chain: Dilute lidocaine numbs and swells fat
angle.text: Tumescent liposuction removes localized fat under local anesthesia, used on the abdomen, flanks, neck and jowls for a slimmer, more defined contour. Dilute lidocaine numbs and swells the fat before it is suctioned out. The change is visible after healing; safety data come from large surgeon surveys.

lead: Tumescent liposuction is a liposuction technique in which large volumes of dilute lidocaine and epinephrine are infiltrated into subcutaneous fat before fat is aspirated through thin cannulas. The solution numbs the area and constricts blood vessels to reduce bleeding, so the procedure can be done under local anesthesia.[1][2] It is credited to dermatologist Jeffrey Klein in the 1980s.[1]

It is a standard approach to body contouring and is also used for lipedema. Safety data come largely from surveys of dermatologic surgeons; a 1999 analysis of deaths and surveys of tens of thousands of procedures have been published, and the main specific concern discussed in the literature is lidocaine dosing.[3][4][5][6]

paras: The tumescent method swells the target fat with infiltrated fluid until it is firm. The fluid contains lidocaine for anesthesia and epinephrine to limit bleeding, allowing patients to remain awake, according to the literature on the technique.[2][3] Wikipedia notes that American dermatologists developed local-anesthetic-only methods in the 1980s, leading to the tumescent technique.[1]

A 1999 New England Journal of Medicine report identified five deaths after tumescent liposuction and noted that, because adverse-event reporting is not mandatory, the true incidence of complications and deaths is unknown; it also observed that recommended lidocaine doses are as high as 55 mg/kg while safety data are scarce.[4]

A 1995 survey of dermatologic surgeons covered 15,336 patients, and a 2002 survey examined office-based tumescent liposuction safety.[3][5] A 2016 analysis estimated maximal safe tumescent lidocaine dosages.[6] Wikipedia states that lidocaine toxicity has been linked to deaths in liposuction and that overall mortality is reported at roughly one per 10,000 cases as of 2011.[1]

A 2012 study reported good long-term results of tumescent liposuction in lipedema, and Dutch guidelines on lipedema were published in 2017.[7][8] Tumescent harvesting is also used to collect adipose tissue for stem-cell and fat-grafting work, and a 2006 study found that harvesting method influenced stem cell yield.[2]

Human data include large surveys of safety, a lipedema outcome study, and pharmacologic studies of lidocaine dosing.[3][5][6][7] Registered trials include a lidocaine maximum-safe-dose study (NCT00977028), a trial of cold versus warm tumescent solution in arm liposculpture (NCT06865911) with 52 participants, and a trial of tranexamic acid in tumescent solution (NCT06648265) with 78 participants.[9][10][11]
